subject: Critical Thinking
title: Act vs. Rule Utilitarianism: Follow the Rule or Break It?
description: A fast breakdown of Act vs. Rule Utilitarianism: Follow the Rule or Break It? for builders.

hook.text: Lying is usually bad. But lying to a murderer about where your friend is hiding? Act utilitarianism says: lie.

buildup.text: Act utilitarianism: evaluate EACH action individually.

discovery.text: Rule utilitarianism: 'If everyone followed this rule, would happiness increase?' 'Don't lie' generally works – even if.

twist.text: Act utilitarianism is more flexible but prone to rationalization: 'THIS lie is justified.' Rule utilitarianism is.

climax.text: Most institutions use rule utilitarianism while individuals use act utilitarianism. Both have trade-offs.

punchline.text: Rules exist because individual calculations fail. But sometimes, rules fail too.

quiz.question: What is the key difference between act and rule utilitarianism?
options: Act utilitarianism evaluates each action individually; rule utilitarianism follows generally beneficial rules

details.summary: Act utilitarianism evaluates each individual action by its consequences, while rule utilitarianism asks which general rules would produce the best outcomes if everyone followed them. The split addresses whether to optimize case by case or through stable principles.
details.whyItMatters: The distinction affects whether you bend rules in exceptional situations or uphold them for long-term societal stability.
takeaways: Act utilitarianism maximizes utility per situation
Rule utilitarianism maximizes utility through consistent rules
Rule versions avoid some objections to act utilitarianism

faq.question: When might act and rule utilitarianism give different answers?
faq.answer: Act utilitarianism might justify lying in a specific case to prevent harm, while rule utilitarianism would oppose it because a universal lying rule undermines trust overall.

faq.question: Which form of utilitarianism is more practical in real life?
faq.answer: Rule utilitarianism is often considered more practical because following reliable rules reduces the cognitive burden of calculating consequences for every single decision.
